claim: SMOC is conserved phylogenetically from vertebrates to arthropods.
source: The matricellular protein SMOC (Secreted Modular Calcium binding protein) is conserved phylogenetically from vertebrates to arthropods.
evidence: This is a statement about phylogenetic conservation presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but is based on established knowledge.

claim: SMOC inhibits bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling downstream of its receptor via activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling.
source: We showed previously that SMOC inhibits bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling downstream of its receptor via activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling.
evidence: This claim references previous work by the authors (Thomas et al., 2009) as cited in the abstract.

claim: The most prominent effect of the Drosophila orthologue pentagone (pent) is expanding the range of BMP signaling during wing patterning.
source: In contrast, the most prominent effect of the Drosophila orthologue, pentagone (pent), is expanding the range of BMP signaling during wing patterning.
evidence: This statement is based on prior literature about pentagone function.

claim: SMOC-∆EC, lacking the extracellular calcium binding (EC) domain, inhibited BMP2 signaling.
source: Using SMOC deletion constructs we found that SMOC-∆EC, lacking the extracellular calcium binding (EC) domain, inhibited BMP2 signaling
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B where SMOC-∆EC inhibits BMP2-induced Smad phosphorylation.

claim: SMOC-EC (EC domain only) enhanced BMP2 signaling.
source: whereas SMOC-EC (EC domain only) enhanced BMP2 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B where SMOC-EC enhances BMP2-induced Smad phosphorylation.

claim: The SMOC-EC domain bound HSPGs with a similar affinity to BMP2.
source: The SMOC-EC domain bound HSPGs with a similar affinity to BMP2
evidence: This claim is supported by heparin-binding studies shown in Figure 5B demonstrating equivalent binding affinities.

claim: SMOC-EC could expand the range of BMP signaling in an in vitro assay by competition for HSPG-binding.
source: and could expand the range of BMP signaling in an in vitro assay by competition for HSPG-binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro diffusion assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: BMPs comprise at least twenty structurally-related members of the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) superfamily.
source: During development bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), comprising at least twenty structurally-related members of the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) superfamily, are involved in many growth and differentiation events essential for determining body structure (Wu and Hill, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Wu and Hill, 2009.

claim: BMPs are involved in many growth and differentiation events essential for determining body structure.
source: During development bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), comprising at least twenty structurally-related members of the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) superfamily, are involved in many growth and differentiation events essential for determining body structure (Wu and Hill, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Wu and Hill, 2009.

claim: Establishing temporospatial gradients or restricted distributions of BMP signaling is important for many developmental processes.
source: Establishing temporospatial gradients or restricted distributions of BMP signaling is important for many of these processes
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: BMP signaling is regulated by ligand binding by extracellular BMP antagonists.
source: which are regulated by a number of mechanisms: ligand binding by extracellular BMP antagonists (Brazil et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Brazil et al., 2015.

claim: BMP signaling is regulated by intracellular feedback inhibition downstream of the BMP receptor.
source: intracellular feedback inhibition downstream of the BMP receptor (Massagué et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited from Massagué et al., 2005.

claim: BMP signaling is regulated by spatially restricted proteolytic processing.
source: spatially restricted proteolytic processing (Thomas et al., 2006)
evidence: This is cited from Thomas et al., 2006.

claim: BMP signaling is regulated by promotion or restriction of diffusion by interactions with extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen type IV.
source: and promotion or restriction of diffusion by interactions with extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen type IV (Umulis et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited from Umulis et al., 2009.

claim: BMP signaling is regulated by interactions with heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs).
source: and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) (Matsumoto et al., 2010; Belenkaya et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Matsumoto et al., 2010 and Belenkaya et al., 2004.

claim: BMP signaling is influenced via communication with other signaling pathways, particularly those that act through mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs).
source: In addition, BMP signaling is also influenced via communication with other signaling pathways, particularly those that act through mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell signaling.

claim: MAPK-directed phosphorylation of BMP receptor-regulated Smad 1/5/8 in the linker region inhibits BMP signaling by blocking Smad translocation to the nucleus.
source: MAPK-directed phosphorylation of BMP receptor-regulated Smad 1/5/8 in the linker region inhibits BMP signaling by blocking Smad translocation to the nucleus (Alarcón et al., 2009; Sapkota et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Alarcón et al., 2009 and Sapkota et al., 2007.

claim: SMOC is a matricellular protein associated with basement membranes.
source: We showed previously that SMOC, a matricellular protein associated with basement membranes (Vannahme et al., 2002)
evidence: This is cited from Vannahme et al., 2002.

claim: SMOC is expressed in developing brain, branchial arches, eye, pronephros, limb bud cartilage condensations, and joint interzones.
source: and expressed in developing brain, branchial arches, eye, pronephros, limb bud cartilage condensations, and joint interzones (Okada et al., 2011; Rainger et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited from Okada et al., 2011; Rainger et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2009.

claim: Following the addition of BMP2 to NIH3T3 fibroblasts transfected with SMOC, downstream phosphorylation of Smad 1/5/8 is blocked.
source: following the addition of BMP2 to NIH3T3 fibroblasts transfected with SMOC, downstream phosphorylation of Smad 1/5/8 is blocked (Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Thomas et al., 2009.

claim: In Xenopus ectodermal explants (animal caps), SMOC was shown to activate MAPK signaling and inhibit Smad 1/5/8-mediated BMP signaling downstream of the constitutively active BMP receptor, BMPR1B.
source: In Xenopus ectodermal explants (animal caps), SMOC was shown to activate MAPK signaling and inhibit Smad 1/5/8-mediated BMP signaling downstream of the constitutively active BMP receptor, BMPR1B (Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Thomas et al., 2009.

claim: BMP inhibition by SMOC results from activation of MAPK signaling and subsequent ubiquitination and degradation of Smad following linker Smad phosphorylation.
source: Although the exact mechanism is not known, the activity was lost in the presence of non-phosphorylatable linker-mutant Smad, suggesting that BMP inhibition results from activation of MAPK signaling and subsequent ubiquitination and degradation of Smad following linker Smad phosphorylation (Sapkota et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations with linker-mutant Smad, citing Sapkota et al., 2007.

claim: In Drosophila, the SMOC orthologue pentagone (pent) is expressed in developing wing imaginal discs.
source: In Drosophila, the SMOC orthologue pentagone (pent) is expressed in developing wing imaginal discs and has also been shown to inhibit BMP signaling (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: Pentagone has been shown to inhibit BMP signaling.
source: In Drosophila, the SMOC orthologue pentagone (pent) is expressed in developing wing imaginal discs and has also been shown to inhibit BMP signaling (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: Pent did not appear to inhibit BMP signaling in the presence of the constitutively active zebrafish BMPR1 receptor, Alk8.
source: However, Pent did not appear to inhibit BMP signaling in the presence of the constitutively active zebrafish BMPR1 receptor, Alk8 (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: SMOC and Pent are structurally similar, containing an N-terminal follistatin-like domain (FS), followed by two thyroglobulin-like domains separated by a non-homologous domain, and a C-terminal extracellular calcium binding (EC) domain.
source: Structurally, SMOC and Pent are similar, containing an N-terminal follistatin-like domain (FS), followed by two thyroglobulin-like domains separated by a non-homologous domain, and a C-terminal extracellular calcium binding (EC) domain (Vannahme et al., 2002; Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vannahme et al., 2002 and Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: Pent contains an additional EC domain located between the two thyroglobulin-like domains.
source: Although Pent contains an additional EC domain located between the two thyroglobulin-like domains, their phylogenetic conservation would predict similar functions.
evidence: This is a structural observation about Pent.

claim: In Drosophila, Pent binds to the cell surface HSPG, Dally.
source: In Drosophila, Pent binds to the cell surface HSPG, Dally, which is required for Pent to extend the range of BMP signaling during Drosophila wing patterning (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: Dally is required for Pent to extend the range of BMP signaling during Drosophila wing patterning.
source: In Drosophila, Pent binds to the cell surface HSPG, Dally, which is required for Pent to extend the range of BMP signaling during Drosophila wing patterning (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: SMOC has been shown to bind to HSPGs.
source: While SMOC has also been shown to bind to HSPGs (Klemenčič et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from Klemenčič et al., 2013.

claim: A pent cDNA construct was biologically active in Drosophila.
source: We first confirmed that a pent cDNA construct was biologically active in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When pent was expressed in its normal location during wing development, using the Gal4/UAS system, the mutant phenotype was rescued completely.
source: When pent was expressed in its normal location during wing development, using the Gal4/UAS system, the mutant phenotype was rescued completely, demonstrating that the pent construct had full biological activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of a synthetic pent mRNA (co-pent) optimized for codon usage and translation efficiency in Xenopus produced a dorsalized phenotype indistinguishable from that observed following overexpression of Xenopus SMOC-1 (XSMOC-1).
source: however overexpression of a synthetic pent mRNA (co-pent) optimized for codon usage and translation efficiency in Xenopus (Villegas and Kropinski, 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) produced a dorsalized phenotype indistinguishable from that observed following overexpression of Xenopus SMOC-1 (XSMOC-1) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with codon optimization cited from Villegas and Kropinski, 2008.

claim: XVent was strongly expressed in animal caps from embryos injected with caBMPR1B alone.
source: As expected, XVent, a direct downstream target of BMP signaling (Gawantka et al., 1995), was strongly expressed in animal caps from embryos injected with caBMPR1B alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with XVent cited as a BMP target from Gawantka et al., 1995.

claim: XVent was markedly reduced in caps from embryos co-injected with caBMPR1B and either co-pent or XSMOC-1.
source: In contrast, XVent was markedly reduced in caps from embryos co-injected with caBMPR1B and either co-pent or XSMOC-1 (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pent can inhibit BMP signaling downstream of the BMPR1B receptor.
source: these results suggested that, as we had shown previously for SMOC (Thomas et al., 2009), Pent can inhibit BMP signaling downstream of the BMPR1B receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the XVent reduction data in Figure 1C and previous work on SMOC.

claim: In order for SMOC/pent to inhibit BMP signaling in the presence of caBMPR1B, SMOC/pent needed to be overexpressed at a 2:1 ratio.
source: Conversely, in order for SMOC/Pent to inhibit BMP signaling in the presence of caBMPR1B, SMOC/pent needed to be overexpressed at a 2:1 ratio (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is based on the experimental conditions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SMOC was not able to inhibit BMP signaling in the presence of an excess of caBMPR1B.
source: SMOC was not able to inhibit BMP signaling in the presence of an excess of caBMPR1B (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Attempts to express XSMOC-1 in Drosophila using a synthetic construct optimized for codon usage in Drosophila were unsuccessful.
source: However, attempts to express XSMOC-1 in Drosophila using a synthetic construct optimized for codon usage in Drosophila were unsuccessful
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: XSMOC-1 was not translated in amounts sufficient to be effective in Drosophila.
source: immunoblot analysis of two Drosophila lines generated to overexpress XSMOC-1 demonstrated that XSMOC-1 was below the level of detection (5 ng) for the assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that despite codon optimization, XSMOC-1 was not translated in amounts sufficient to be effective.
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When first expressed, two predominant induced proteins were observed on SDS-PAGE; one migrating at 49 kDa, the other at approximately 24 kDa.
source: When first expressed, two predominant induced proteins were observed on SDS-PAGE (Figure 2A); one migrating at 49 kDa, the other at approximately 24 kDa.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Protein sequencing revealed the 49 kDa protein to be XSMOC-1, whereas the 24 kDa protein was a partial XSMOC-1 sequence beginning at V235.
source: Protein sequencing revealed the 49 kDa protein to be XSMOC-1, whereas the 24 kDa protein was a partial XSMOC-1 sequence beginning at V235.
evidence: This is based on protein sequencing data.

claim: The base sequence (GTG) at V235 was consistent with an alternative start codon.
source: The base sequence (GTG) was consistent with an alternative start codon (Villegas and Kropinski, 2008)
evidence: This is cited from Villegas and Kropinski, 2008.

claim: When GTG at V235 was changed to GTA by site-directed mutagenesis only the expected 49 kDa product was produced.
source: when changed to GTA by site-directed mutagenesis only the expected 49 kDa product was produced (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Initial XSMOC-1 refolding studies using the protocol where calcium is absent produced hSMOC-1 that is monomeric.
source: Initial XSMOC-1 refolding studies were conducted using the protocol described previously, where calcium is absent, and produces hSMOC-1 that is monomeric (Novinec et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Novinec et al., 2008.

claim: Analysis by S-200 size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) showed a mixture of poorly separated peaks, one of which had a calculated molecular weight of 45.5 kDa, approximate to the predicted 49.6 kDa of monomeric XSMOC-1.
source: Analysis by S-200 size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) showed a mixture of poorly separated peaks, one of which had a calculated molecular weight of 45.5 kDa, approximate to the predicted 49.6 kDa of monomeric XSMOC-1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: XSMOC-1 refolded in the absence of calcium was inactive in the Xenopus animal cap assay.
source: However, when tested in the Xenopus animal cap assay the protein was inactive (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: When refolded in the presence of 2 mM CaCl2, both XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1∆EC migrated as single, symmetrical peaks with calculated molecular weights approximately twice the predicted monomeric sizes.
source: With this change, in addition to poorly-separated higher molecular weight material, both XSMOC-1 (Figure 2C) and XSMOC-1∆EC (Figure 2D) migrated as single, symmetrical peaks. Their calculated molecular weights of 95.4 kDa and 53 kDa, respectively, were approximately twice the predicted monomeric sizes (49.6 kDa and 32.3 kDa).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-∆EC refolded in the presence of calcium form dimers.
source: This suggested that XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-∆EC refolded in the presence of calcium form dimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC molecular weight data.

claim: hSMOC-1 migrated as an apparent dimer under refolding conditions with calcium with a calculated molecular weight of 90.3 kDa.
source: Furthermore, hSMOC-1, shown previously to elute as a monomer (Novinec et al., 2008), also migrated as an apparent dimer under these conditions with a calculated molecular weight of 90.3 kDa (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and contrasts with previous findings from Novinec et al., 2008.

claim: XSMOC-1EC eluted at the calculated molecular weight of 23.7 kDa, consistent with that predicted for a monomer (18.4 kDa).
source: In contrast, XSMOC-1EC eluted at the calculated molecular weight of 23.7 kDa (Figure 2E), consistent with that predicted for a monomer (18.4 kDa).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Dimeric XSMOC-1 could not be dissociated by chelation of Ca++ ions and continued to elute as a dimer following dialysis in the presence of 10.5 mM EDTA.
source: Dimeric XSMOC-1 could not be dissociated by chelation of Ca++ ions and continued to elute as a dimer following dialysis in the presence of 10.5 mM EDTA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dimeric XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-∆EC were not formed through disulfide linkages.
source: Analysis by SDS-PAGE under non-reducing and reducing conditions demonstrated that dimeric XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-∆EC were not formed through disulfide linkages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1∆EC induced anterior neural markers in Xenopus animal cap explants, but XSMOC-1EC did not.
source: RT-PCR demonstrated the induction of anterior neural markers in the presence of XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1∆EC, but not XSMOC-1EC (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: hSMOC-1 was effective in inducing anterior neural markers in the Xenopus animal cap assay.
source: hSMOC-1 was also effective in this assay (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The optimal concentration of SMOC for neural induction was found to be 100 μg/ml.
source: For these studies, the optimal concentration of SMOC was found to be 100 μg/ml
evidence: This is based on experimental optimization.

claim: A two-hour pulse of XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1∆EC protein was sufficient to commit the naïve ectoderm of the Xenopus animal cap to an anterior neural fate sixteen hours later.
source: Temporal analyses showed that a two-hour pulse of XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1∆EC protein was sufficient to commit the naïve ectoderm of the Xenopus animal cap to an anterior neural fate sixteen hours later (Figure 3B)

claim: A one-hour pulse of XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1∆EC was not sufficient to commit the naïve ectoderm to an anterior neural fate.
source: a one-hour pulse was not.

claim: Inhibition of endogenous BMP activity in Xenopus ectodermal explants promotes a neural fate.
source: While it is well established that inhibition of endogenous BMP activity in Xenopus ectodermal explants promotes a neural fate (Vonica and Brivanlou, 2006)

claim: BMP2 treatment alone caused phosphorylation of Smad 1/5/8 in NIH-3T3 and HEK-293 cells.
source: As expected, BMP2 treatment alone caused phosphorylation of Smad 1/5/8 (Figure 4A,B).

claim: BMP2-induced Smad 1/5/8 phosphorylation was blocked in the presence of XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1∆EC.
source: This was blocked in the presence of XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1∆EC

claim: XSMOC-1EC significantly enhanced BMP2-mediated Smad phosphorylation.
source: whereas XSMOC-1EC significantly enhanced BMP2-mediated Smad phosphorylation (Figure 4A,B).

claim: The addition of XSMOC-1EC alone to NIH-3T3 cells did not result in Smad1/5/8 phosphorylation.
source: Potentiation of Smad phosphorylation by the EC domain was not due to an additive effect, as the addition of XSMOC-1EC alone to NIH-3T3 cells did not result in Smad1/5/8 phosphorylation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The induction of XVent by caBMPRIB was blocked by co-expression with XSMOC-1, XSMOC-1∆FS, or XSMOC-1∆EC.
source: Analysis of animal caps following co-injection of Xenopus embryos with caBMPRIB and XSMOC-1, XSMOC-1∆FS, or XSMOC-1∆EC showed inhibition of BMP signaling, indicated by the suppression of XVent expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpression of XSMOC-1Tg1, containing the Tg1-like domains only, did not inhibit BMP signaling.
source: Whereas these data suggest that the FS and EC domains are not required for BMP inhibition overexpression of XSMOC-1Tg1, containing the Tg1-like domains only, did not inhibit BMP signaling in this assay (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Deletion of the Tg1-like domains (XSMOC-1∆Tg1) did not inhibit BMP signaling.
source: deletion of the Tg1-like domains (XSMOC-1∆Tg1) produced a similar result.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Misfolding of the protein produced by XSMOC-1∆FS∆EC is the most likely reason for the inability of this construct to block BMP signaling.
source: Consequently, we consider misfolding of the protein produced by XSMOC-1∆FS∆EC as the most likely reason for the inability of this construct to block BMP signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known effects of large deletions on protein folding.

claim: The phenotype of anopthalmia, oligodactyly, and joint abnormalities was found to be the same in patients with nonsense or frameshift mutations and those with missense mutations in the second Tg1-like domain.
source: The phenotype of anopthalmia, oligodactyly, and joint abnormalities was found to be the same in patients with nonsense or frameshift mutations and those with missense mutations in the second Tg1-like domain (Rainger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Rainger et al., 2011.

claim: The two pedigrees harboring two different single amino acid missense mutations in the Tg1-like domain suggests this domain is essential for SMOC-1 function.
source: As the nonsense and frameshift mutations were predicted to result in a complete loss of SMOC-1 function, the two pedigrees harboring two different single amino acid missense mutations in the Tg1-like domain suggests this domain is indeed essential for SMOC-1 function.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic data from Rainger et al., 2011.

claim: SMOC and BMP2 co-purify following heparin affinity chromatography of bovine cartilage extracts.
source: The binding of SMOC/Pent and BMP2/4 to HSPGs is known, as evidenced by the co-purification of SMOC and BMPs following heparin affinity chromatography of bovine cartilage extracts (Chang et al., 1994)
evidence: This is cited from Chang et al., 1994.

claim: BMP2/4 and the EC domain of hSMOC/Pent bind to heparin/HSPGs.
source: and the binding of BMP2/4 and the EC domain of hSMOC/Pent to heparin/HSPGs (Vuilleumier et al., 2010; Klemenčič et al., 2013; Ruppert et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010; Klemenčič et al., 2013; Ruppert et al., 1996.

claim: The basic amino acid-rich putative heparin-binding region identified within the EC domain of SMOC is highly conserved in Pent.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and cited from Klemenčič et al., 2013.

claim: XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1EC bound to heparin Sepharose in the presence of 0.5M NaCl, whereas XSMOC-1∆EC did not.

claim: The EC domain is the site of HSPG binding in SMOC.
source: XSMOC-1 and XSMOC-1EC bound to heparin Sepharose in the presence of 0.5M NaCl, whereas XSMOC-1∆EC did not (Figure 5A), confirming the EC domain to be the site of HSPG binding.
evidence: This is confirmed by the heparin-binding data in Figure 5A.

claim: XSMOC-1EC and BMP2 have similar heparin-binding affinities, with both eluting between 0.65M and 0.7M NaCl.
source: Comparison of the heparin-binding affinities of XSMOC-1EC and BMP2 showed a striking similarity, with both eluting between 0.65M and 0.7M NaCl (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: XSMOC-1 and BMP2 do not bind to each other.
source: The possibility that XSMOC-1 and BMP2 bind to each other was discounted (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When BMP2 was incubated with XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1 EC, pre-bound to heparin-Sepharose, BMP2 was only present in the unbound fraction and did not co-elute with XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1 EC.
source: when BMP2 was incubated with XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1 EC, pre-bound to heparin-Sepharose, BMP2 was only present in the unbound fraction (Figure 5C; lanes 2 and 5) and did not co-elute with XSMOC-1 or XSMOC-1 EC (Figure 5C; lanes 3 and 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The lack of interaction of SMOC with BMP2 agrees with an analogous finding observed for Pent and the Drosophila BMP, decapentaplegic (Dpp).
source: The lack of interaction of SMOC with BMP2 agrees with an analogous finding observed for Pent and the Drosophila BMP, decapentaplegic (Dpp) (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: XSMOC-1EC could compete with BMPs for HSPG binding on HEK293 cells and thereby increase BMP bioavailability.
source: This, combined with SMOC and BMP2 having similar heparin-binding affinities, suggests that XSMOC-1EC could compete with BMPs for HSPG binding on HEK293 cells and thereby increase BMP bioavailability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar binding affinities shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only a few luciferase positive cells (8%) were detected adjacent to agarose gel containing HS.

evidence: This is shown in Figures 6B and 6E.

claim: When the matrix contained both HS and XSMOC-1EC, the number of BMP-responsive cells (64%) was similar to that observed in the absence of HS.

evidence: This is shown in Figures 6C and 6F.

claim: Binding of BMPs to HSPGs restricts their range of effect.
source: The assay demonstrated that binding of BMPs to HSPGs restricts their range of effect
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro diffusion assay results shown in Figure 6.

claim: BMP diffusion can be enhanced by the binding of SMOC to HSPGs, effectively expanding the range of effect.
source: and that BMP diffusion can be enhanced by the binding of SMOC to HSPGs, effectively expanding the range of effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro diffusion assay results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Injection of 30 pg BMP2 mRNA at the two cell stage was sufficient to induce BMP signaling in the host tissue, while pSmad was observed only at a few cell diameters into the donor graft.
source: Following a series of titration experiments we found that injection of 30 pg BMP2 mRNA at the two cell stage (15 pg into each blastomere) was sufficient to induce BMP signaling in the host tissue, while pSmad was observed only at a few cell diameters into the donor graft (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Donor caps from embryos injected with a low amount of SMOC mRNA (10 pg) had an increased number of pSmad positive nuclei compared to non-SMOC injected caps.
source: Donor caps from embryos injected with a low amount of SMOC mRNA (10 pg) had an increased number of pSmad positive nuclei compared to non-SMOC injected caps (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Donor caps from embryos injected with a high amount of SMOC mRNA (300 pg) were devoid of pSmad.
source: Conversely, donor caps from embryos injected with a high amount of SMOC mRNA (300 pg) were devoid of pSmad (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In an intact tissue, low concentrations of SMOC can promote diffusion of BMP from its source of synthesis, thereby extending its range of effect.
source: The results demonstrate that, in an intact tissue, low concentrations of SMOC can promote diffusion of BMP from its source of synthesis, thereby extending its range of effect
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo conjugate assay results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: High SMOC concentrations inhibit BMP signaling.
source: whereas high SMOC concentrations inhibit BMP signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo conjugate assay results shown in Figure 7F.

claim: BMP signaling was both absent in the graft expressing the highest level of SMOC and decreased in the BMP2-expressing ectoderm immediately adjacent to the SMOC expressing graft.
source: Closer examination of the host tissue surrounding the donor grafts expressing the highest level of SMOC showed BMP signaling was both absent in the graft and decreased in the BMP2-expressing ectoderm immediately adjacent to the SMOC expressing graft (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: SMOC inhibits BMP signaling within the graft and also diffuses into the immediate adjacent tissue at levels sufficient to inhibit BMP signaling.
source: This would be consistent with SMOC inhibiting BMP signaling within the graft and also diffusing into the immediate adjacent tissue at levels sufficient to inhibit BMP signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation in Figure 7F.

claim: During Drosophila wing development, while dpp expression is restricted to a stripe of medial cells in the wing disc, the morphogenetic gradient expands across the anterior/posterior (A/P) axis.
source: During Drosophila wing development, while dpp expression is restricted to a stripe of medial cells in the wing disc, the morphogenetic gradient expands across the anterior/posterior (A/P) axis (Nellen et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from Nellen et al., 1996.

claim: Long-range Dpp signaling in the wing has been shown to involve both pent and the cell membrane-anchored HSPG, dally.
source: Long-range Dpp signaling in the wing has been shown to involve both pent and the cell membrane-anchored HSPG, dally (Vuilleumier et al., 2010; Fujise et al., 2003)
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010 and Fujise et al., 2003.

claim: The absence of either pent or dally causes severe contraction of the range of Dpp signaling, and wing patterning defects.
source: the absence of either causes severe contraction of the range of Dpp signaling, and wing patterning defects (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: When XSMOC-1EC is added to HEK293 cells at 50 μg/ml, in serum-free media it will bind to the many cell surface HSPG binding sites.
source: When XSMOC-1EC is added to HEK293 cells at 50 μg/ml, in serum-free media it will bind to the many cell surface HSPG binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known HSPG-binding properties of XSMOC-1EC.

claim: A potentiation of BMP signaling was observed when XSMOC-1EC was added to HEK293 cells followed by BMP2.
source: Consequently, following the subsequent addition of BMP2, any impairment of BMP2/receptor affinity caused by SMOC/HSPG binding would result in a reduction of BMP signaling. Instead, a potentiation of BMP signaling was observed (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Dally is expressed both medially and laterally in the wing disc.
source: Dally, expressed both medially and laterally in the wing disc (Fujise et al., 2003)
evidence: This is cited from Fujise et al., 2003.

claim: Dally encodes a cell autonomous membrane-associated protein.
source: Dally, expressed both medially and laterally in the wing disc (Fujise et al., 2003), encodes a cell autonomous membrane-associated protein
evidence: This is established knowledge about Dally.

claim: Pent is expressed laterally in the wing disc.
source: pent, expressed laterally
evidence: This is based on expression pattern data.

claim: Dpp is expressed medially in the wing disc.
source: and dpp, expressed medially
evidence: This is based on expression pattern data.

claim: Pent and dpp encode secreted proteins able to diffuse away from their source.
source: pent, expressed laterally, and dpp, expressed medially, encode secreted proteins able to diffuse away from their source (Thomas et al., 2009; Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Thomas et al., 2009 and Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: SMOC can diffuse across many cell diameters in Xenopus animal caps.
source: Indeed, we showed previously that SMOC can diffuse across many cell diameters in Xenopus animal caps (Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Thomas et al., 2009.

claim: At the lateral border, Dpp signaling will be inhibited by a combination of the expression of pent and the BMP repressor, brinker.
source: At the lateral border, Dpp signaling will be inhibited by a combination of the expression of pent (Figure 7A) and the BMP repressor, brinker (Minami et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference based on known expression patterns and cited from Minami et al., 1999.

claim: As Pent diffuses across the wing disc it will create a lateral-medial gradient.
source: As Pent diffuses across the wing disc it will create a lateral-medial gradient
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and diffusion properties of Pent.

claim: At low levels, Pent will occupy some Dally binding sites, promoting further Dpp diffusion.
source: At low levels, Pent will occupy some Dally binding sites, promoting further Dpp diffusion
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: At high levels, Pent will occupy many Dally binding sites and also inhibit Dpp signaling downstream of its receptor.
source: at high levels, Pent will occupy many Dally binding sites and also inhibit Dpp signaling downstream of its receptor (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: In the absence of pent, medial-lateral diffusion of Dpp will be restricted by Dally because there is no Pent to compete for Dally binding sites.
source: In the absence of pent, medial-lateral diffusion of Dpp will be restricted by Dally because there is no Pent to compete for Dally binding sites (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on mutant phenotypes.

claim: The high level of medially localized Dpp signaling, indicated by Mad phosphorylation (pMad), has been shown to induce expression of the inhibitory Smad, daughters against dpp (dad), promoting a negative feedback loop to limit the range of Dpp signaling.
source: The resulting high level of medially localized Dpp signaling, indicated by Mad phosphorylation (pMad) (Vuilleumier et al., 2010), has been shown to induce expression of the inhibitory Smad, daughters against dpp (dad), promoting a negative feedback loop to limit the range of Dpp signaling (Tsuneizumi et al., 1997; Ogiso et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010; Tsuneizumi et al., 1997; Ogiso et al., 2011.

claim: In the absence of dally, Dpp diffusion will be restricted as Dally-binding is required to establish both Dpp and Pent gradients.
source: In the absence of dally, Dpp diffusion will also be restricted as Dally-binding is required to establish both Dpp and Pent gradients (Vuilleumier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Vuilleumier et al., 2010.

claim: Medially, dally mutant discs show abnormally high levels of pMad.
source: Medially, dally mutant discs show abnormally high levels of pMad (Fujise et al., 2003)
evidence: This is cited from Fujise et al., 2003.

claim: The proposed mode of action of Pent in the Drosophila wing disc is consistent with the role of glypicans in the 'restricted extracellular diffusion' model for establishing a Dpp signaling gradient.
source: Our proposed mode of action of Pent in the Drosophila wing disc is consistent with the role of glypicans in the 'restricted extracellular diffusion' model for establishing a Dpp signaling gradient (Schwank et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from Schwank et al., 2011.

claim: Binding of Pent to Dally in Drosophila induces endocytosis of the complex, effectively reducing the amount of Dally on cell surfaces.
source: During the review of this manuscript a study was published (Norman et al., 2016) showing that binding of Pent to Dally in Drosophila induces endocytosis of the complex, effectively reducing the amount of Dally on cell surfaces.
evidence: This is cited from Norman et al., 2016.

claim: Both competitive binding of SMOC/Pent to HSPGs and removal of HSPG binding sites for BMP/Dpp by endocytosis would promote BMP/Dpp diffusion.
source: Although it remains to be determined whether binding of SMOC to HSPGs also induces endocytosis, this finding is consistent with the model we propose: both competitive binding of SMOC/Pent to HSPGs and removal of HSPG binding sites for BMP/Dpp by endocytosis would promote BMP/Dpp diffusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Norman et al., 2016 findings and the authors' model.

claim: Removal of the heparin binding site within BMP4 has been shown to promote the BMP diffusion in Xenopus embryos.
source: This idea is further supported by the observation that removal of the heparin binding site within BMP4 has also been shown to promote the BMP diffusion in Xenopus embryos (Ohkawara et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Ohkawara et al., 2002.

claim: The binding of Pent to Dally modulates Wingless (Wg) signaling in Drosophila, where a reduction in Wg signaling is observed in the presence of high levels of Pent.
source: The binding of Pent to Dally also modulates Wingless (Wg) signaling in Drosophila, where a reduction in Wg signaling is observed in the presence of high levels of Pent (Norman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Norman et al., 2016.

claim: The interaction of Wg with Dally is known to potentiate Wg binding to its receptor Frizzled.
source: The interaction of Wg with Dally is known to potentiate Wg binding to its receptor Frizzled (Tsuda et al., 1999; Lin and Perrimon, 1999)
evidence: This is cited from Tsuda et al., 1999 and Lin and Perrimon, 1999.

claim: The sequestration of Dally by Pent would be consistent with a reduction in Wg signaling.
source: therefore, the sequestration of Dally by Pent would be consistent with a reduction in Wg signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known interaction of Wg with Dally.

claim: Linker Smad phosphorylation at MAPK sites has been shown to be followed by phosphorylation at Glycogen Synthase Kinase 3 (GSK3) sites, resulting in Smad ubiquitination and degradation.
source: Linker Smad phosphorylation at MAPK sites has been shown to be followed by phosphorylation at Glycogen Synthase Kinase 3 (GSK3) sites (Fuentealba et al., 2007), resulting in Smad ubiquitination and degradation (Sapkota et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Fuentealba et al., 2007 and Sapkota et al., 2007.

claim: The activity of GSK3 is inhibited by Wnt signaling.
source: As the activity of GSK3 is inhibited by Wnt signaling
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell signaling.

claim: A reduction in Wnt signaling by Pent/SMOC could potentiate GSK3-mediated phosphorylation of linker Smad.
source: a reduction in Wnt signaling by Pent/SMOC could potentiate GSK3-mediated phosphorylation of linker Smad.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between Wnt signaling and GSK3 activity.

claim: SMOC-1, GDF5, BMP2/4, and HSPGs are all expressed at the sites of future joint interzones.
source: SMOC-1 (Okada et al., 2011), the cartilage-specific BMP called growth and differentiation factor 5 (GDF5) (Storm and Kingsley, 1996) or cartilage-derived morphogenetic protein-1 (CDMP-1) (Chang et al., 1994), BMP2/4 (Francis-West et al., 1999), and HSPGs (Koyama et al., 1995) are all expressed at the sites of future joint interzones
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Okada et al., 2011; Storm and Kingsley, 1996; Chang et al., 1994; Francis-West et al., 1999; Koyama et al., 1995.

claim: The absence of SMOC-1, GDF5, BMP2/4, or HSPGs results in dysmorphogenesis of autopod joints.
source: the absence of any one of these results in dysmorphogenesis of autopod joints (Okada et al., 2011; Rainger et al., 2011; Chang et al., 1994; Storm and Kingsley, 1996; Mundy et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 1996, 1997).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Okada et al., 2011; Rainger et al., 2011; Chang et al., 1994; Storm and Kingsley, 1996; Mundy et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 1996, 1997.

claim: Joint development in the digits occurs by segmentation of existing cartilage anlagen in regions where BMP signaling is inhibited by the BMP antagonist Chordin.
source: Joint development in the digits occurs by segmentation of existing cartilage anlagen in regions where BMP signaling is inhibited by the BMP antagonist Chordin (Francis-West et al., 1999) and, based on our studies, by SMOC.
evidence: This is cited from Francis-West et al., 1999 and based on the authors' studies.

claim: Once formed, the joint interzone acts as a signaling center to promote appositional growth of the opposing cartilage epipheses.
source: Once formed, the joint interzone acts as a signaling center to promote appositional growth of the opposing cartilage epipheses (Archer et al., 2003; Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Archer et al., 2003 and Ray et al., 2015.

claim: Chordin binds to HSPGs.
source: Within the interzone, Chordin and SMOC will both bind to HSPGs (Klemenčič et al., 2013; Jasuja et al., 2004)
evidence: This is cited from Jasuja et al., 2004.

claim: Binding of Chordin to HSPGs is necessary for its BMP inhibitory activity.
source: Ext1 is essential for HS synthesis and binding of Chordin to HSPGs and is necessary for its BMP inhibitory activity (Jasuja et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Jasuja et al., 2004.

claim: In the absence of HS within the interzone, the BMP antagonist activity of Chordin will be reduced.
source: Consequently, in the absence of HS within the interzone, the BMP antagonist activity of Chordin will be reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement of HS for Chordin activity.

claim: In the absence of HS, there is an increase in BMP signaling (pSmad) observed within the interzone.
source: While SMOC will still contribute to the inhibition of BMP signaling, the imbalance caused by the reduced Chordin activity is consistent with the increase in BMP signaling (pSmad) observed within the interzone in the absence of HS (Mundy et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from Mundy et al., 2011.

claim: In response to BMP signaling, the interzone cells undergo chondrogenesis and the joint does not form (synostosis) in the absence of HS.
source: as a result, in response to BMP signaling, the interzone cells undergo chondrogenesis and the joint does not form (synostosis).
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased BMP signaling in the absence of HS.

claim: In the absence of SMOC, the increased availability of HSPG binding sites will restrict diffusion of GDF/BMPs out of the interzone.
source: In the absence of SMOC, we predict that the increased availability of HSPG binding sites will restrict diffusion of GDF/BMPs out of the interzone.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: Oligodactyly and joint synostosis are observed in patients with Ophthalmo-Acromelic (Waardenburg Anophthalmia) Syndrome.
source: This hypothesis is supported by oligodactyly and joint synostosis observed in patients with Ophthalmo-Acromelic (Waardenburg Anophthalmia) Syndrome (Okada et al., 2011; Rainger et al., 2011; Abouzeid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Okada et al., 2011; Rainger et al., 2011; Abouzeid et al., 2011.

claim: SMOC/Pent can inhibit BMP signaling locally, downstream of the BMP receptor, probably via the region containing the two Tg1-like domains.
source: SMOC/Pent can inhibit BMP signaling locally, downstream of the BMP receptor, probably via the region containing the two Tg1-like domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of SMOC/Pent to cell surface HSPGs via the C-terminal EC domain prevents BMP binding, promoting BMP diffusion, thereby expanding its morphogenetic field.
source: In addition, binding of SMOC/Pent to cell surface HSPGs via the C-terminal EC domain prevents BMP binding, promoting BMP diffusion, thereby expanding its morphogenetic field.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
